def-sel-aic-bic.title: AIC and BIC
def-sel-aic-bic.html: For a model with dk free parameters and maximized log-likelihood ℓk, AICk=−2ℓk+2dk,BICk=−2ℓk+dklog⁡n. In the normal linear model with unknown variance, dk=pk+1 and −2ℓk=nlog⁡(2πSSEk/n)+n (@thm-opt-mle), so up to a constant common to all candidates, AICk=nlog⁡SSEkn+2(pk+1),BICk=nlog⁡SSEkn+(pk+1)log⁡n.{#eq-sel-aic-normal}

def-sel-cp.title: Mallows’ C_p
def-sel-cp.title_html: Mallows’ Cp
def-sel-cp.html: The Cp statistic of candidate k is Ck=SSEks2−n+2pk.

def-sel-cv.title: Cross-validation
def-sel-cv.html: Let the cases (x(i),yi), i=1,…,n, be divided into K disjoint folds I1,…,IK. For each k, let f^(−k) be the prediction rule obtained by applying the procedure to the cases outside Ik. The K-fold cross-validation estimate of prediction error is CVK=1n∑k=1K∑i∈Ik(yi−f^(−k)(x(i)))2. With K=n, each fold is a single case, and CVn is leave-one-out cross-validation. With K=2 and one fold used only for fitting, the estimate is a holdout or validation-set estimate.

def-sel-df.title: Degrees of freedom
def-sel-df.html: The degrees of freedom of a fitting procedure 𝛍μ^ under @eq-sel-model is 𝛍df(μ^)=1σ2∑i=1nCov(μ^i,Yi), so that 𝛍ω=2σ2df(μ^)/n.

def-sel-gcv.title: Generalized cross-validation
def-sel-gcv.html: For a linear smoother y^=Sy with tr(S)<n, GCV=n−1‖y−y^‖2(1−tr(S)/n)2.

def-sel-prediction-error.title: Training error, prediction error, optimism
def-sel-prediction-error.html:
Let 𝛍𝛆Y∗=μ+ε∗, where 𝛆ε∗ is independent of 𝛆ε and has the same distribution: new responses at the same design points. For a fitting procedure 𝛍μ^:

  1. the training error is 𝛍err―=n−1‖Y−μ^‖2;

  2. the in-sample prediction error is 𝛍Errin=n−1E(‖Y∗−μ^‖2|Y);

  3. the optimism is Errin−err―, and its mean ω=E(Errin−err―) is the expected optimism.

def-sel-stepwise.title: Stepwise selection
def-sel-stepwise.html:
Let the current subset be S, with pS columns including the intercept.

  1. Forward selection starts from the intercept alone. At each step it adds the column j∉S that most reduces SSE, provided its F-to-enter Fj=(SSES−SSES+j)/{SSES+j/(n−pS−1)} exceeds a threshold Fin, and stops otherwise.

  2. Backward elimination starts from the full model. At each step it removes the column j∈S with the smallest F-to-remove Fj=(SSES−j−SSES)/{SSES/(n−pS)}, provided this is below a threshold Fout, and stops otherwise.

  3. Stepwise regression (Efroymson 1960) alternates: after each forward step it removes any column whose F-to-remove has fallen below Fout, with Fout≤Fin.

The thresholds may be replaced by a criterion: add or remove the column that lowers AIC (or Cp, or BIC) most, and stop when no move lowers it.

eq-sel-aic-normal.html: AICk=nlog⁡SSEkn+2(pk+1),BICk=nlog⁡SSEkn+(pk+1)log⁡n.

eq-sel-aicc.html: AICck=−2ℓk+2(pk+1)+2(pk+1)(pk+2)n−pk−2

eq-sel-covariance-penalty.html: 𝛍Err^in=err―+2σ2ndf(μ^)

eq-sel-err-in.html: 𝛍𝛍Errin=σ2+1n‖μ^−μ‖2.

eq-sel-hard-risk.html: R(θ;c)=θ2D+1−D+(c−θ)ϕ(c−θ)+(c+θ)ϕ(c+θ),D=Φ(c−θ)−Φ(−c−θ),

eq-sel-loo-shortcut.html: CVn=1n∑i=1n(yi−y^i1−sii)2.

eq-sel-model.html: 𝛍𝛆𝛆𝛆Y=μ+ε,E(ε)=0,Cov(ε)=σ2In,

eq-sel-scaled-risk.html: 𝛍𝛍𝛍Jk=E‖μ^k−μ‖2σ2=pk+γk,γk=‖(I−Mk)μ‖2σ2,

exm-sel-aic-bic.title: Consistency against efficiency
exm-sel-aic-bic.html:
Panel (a) of Figure 29.2.2 uses six independent normal regressors, three of them with slopes 1, 0.5 and 0.25 and three with slope zero, and all 64 subsets as candidates. With n=50 the true subset is found by AIC with probability 0.28 and by BIC with probability 0.24, because the smallest slope is hard to detect. With n=3200 BIC finds it with probability 0.99, while AIC stays at 0.60. That is the limit Pr{χ2(1)≤2}3=0.598, because in large samples AIC keeps each irrelevant regressor independently when its squared t statistic exceeds about 2.

In panel (b) the truth has 1000 regressors with slopes 2/j, all nonzero, and the candidates are the nested models containing the first k regressors, k≤n/4. No candidate is correct. The ratio of the loss of the chosen model to the smallest loss among the candidates falls for AIC, from 1.18 at n=100 to 1.07 at n=3200, while for BIC it stays between 1.3 and 1.8 at every sample size.

exm-sel-branch-bound.title: How much branch and bound saves
exm-sel-branch-bound.title_html: How much branch and bound saves
exm-sel-branch-bound.html: Take n=100 cases and m=15 independent normal regressors, five with nonzero slopes (1,−0.8,0.6,0.4,0.3) and ten with zero slopes. Exhaustive search evaluates 32768 subsets. The branch and bound of @prp-sel-branch-bound finds the same Cp-best subset, with 6 regressors (the four largest slopes and two irrelevant columns), after 1110 evaluations, a fraction 0.034 of the work.

exm-sel-compare.title: Selection procedures in a simulation
exm-sel-compare.html:
Take n=60 cases of eight normal regressors with all pairwise correlations 0.5, σ=1, an intercept, and three nonzero slopes, either weak (1,0.5,0.25) or strong (1,0.8,0.6). Each procedure is scored by its loss at the design points, 𝛃𝛃‖X(β^−β)‖2/σ2, with the intercept’s expected contribution 1 included. Over 2000 data sets:

Weak slopes:

procedure loss Pr(true) size
least squares, all eight 8.98 0.00 8.00
true subset (oracle) 3.97 1.00 3.00
all subsets, AIC 7.81 0.18 3.42
all subsets, BIC 7.33 0.18 2.52
all subsets, leave-one-out 7.76 0.19 3.34
forward, AIC 7.70 0.19 3.34
backward, AIC 7.89 0.17 3.50

Strong slopes:

procedure loss Pr(true) size
least squares, all eight 9.02 0.00 8.00
true subset (oracle) 4.06 1.00 3.00
all subsets, AIC 7.27 0.37 3.93
all subsets, BIC 6.17 0.70 3.20
all subsets, leave-one-out 7.17 0.39 3.85
forward, AIC 7.16 0.39 3.86
backward, AIC 7.35 0.35 3.98

Every selection rule beats least squares on all eight regressors, whose expected loss is 9 (@thm-sel-optimism(c)), but none comes close to the oracle’s 4. The search method hardly matters: forward selection by AIC returned the all-subsets AIC choice in a fraction 0.95 of the weak data sets and 0.96 of the strong ones. The criterion matters more: with strong effects BIC finds the true subset in a fraction 0.70 of data sets and has the smallest loss, while with a weak third slope every rule usually misses it, BIC keeping 2.52 regressors on average.

exm-sel-cv-bias.title: Bias and spread of K-fold cross-validation
exm-sel-cv-bias.title_html: Bias and spread of K-fold cross-validation
exm-sel-cv-bias.html:
Take n=40 cases with k=10 independent standard normal regressors, an intercept, slopes 0.5 and σ=1, and fit by least squares. The target is Err(40)=1.391. Over 4000 training sets, the averages of CVK for K=2,5,10,40 are 2.378, 1.551, 1.461 and 1.408, against Err(n−n/K) of 2.363, 1.547, 1.456 and 1.406 from @prp-sel-cv-target. Fitting to half the data inflates the error by 70% here, because ten slopes are estimated from twenty cases. Their standard deviations across training sets are 1.062, 0.477, 0.411 and 0.378. For this stable procedure leave-one-out has both the smallest bias and the smallest variance.

The error of the fitted model itself, 𝛃𝛃σ2+‖β^−β‖2 for a new standard normal case, varies too: its mean is 1.395 and its standard deviation 0.203. Panel (b) of Figure 29.3.1 plots CV10 against it. The correlation is −0.005 (−0.014 for leave-one-out). Cross-validation reports how well least squares does on average with forty such cases, not how well this fit will do.

exm-sel-forward-miss.title: A pair that forward selection cannot find
exm-sel-forward-miss.title_html: A pair that forward selection cannot find
exm-sel-forward-miss.html: Take n=60 cases of three regressors, x1 and x2 with sample correlation 0.96 and x3 independent of both, and let 𝛆y=3(x1−x2)+0.4x3+ε. The signal lies mostly in the difference x1−x2, a direction in which the regressors vary little. The sample correlations of y with x1, x2 and x3 are −0.02, −0.19 and 0.41. Forward selection enters x3 first and then x2, reaching R2=0.19. The best pair is {x1,x2}, with R2=0.39. Neither of its members looks useful alone, so a procedure that adds one column at a time never sees it. Backward elimination starts from a model that contains the pair and can keep it, but it has blind spots of its own (@exr-sel-not-nested) and cannot start when m≥n.

exm-sel-freedman.title: Freedman’s paradox
exm-sel-freedman.html: Freedman (1983) described the following procedure, which many analyses follow in some form. Fit n=100 cases on 50 regressors, none of which is related to the response. Keep those with p-value below 0.25, refit on the survivors, and report. In one simulated data set 15 regressors survive the first pass, 7 of them are significant at 5% in the refit, and the overall F test of the refit has p-value 0.0030. Over 2000 data sets, an average of 12.3 regressors survive and 5.6 are significant, and the overall F test rejects at 5% in a fraction 0.94 of them. Pure noise produces a model that every standard test endorses.

exm-sel-instability.title: Bootstrapping the state regressions
exm-sel-instability.html: Resample the 50 states with replacement (the case bootstrap of Section 23.1) 1000 times and repeat the all-subsets AIC and BIC choices on each resample. AIC chooses 27 different subsets of the 32 and BIC 25. The AIC choice for the original data, single parenthood and urbanization, is chosen in a fraction 0.15 of resamples, and the most frequent AIC choice, poverty with single parenthood and urbanization, in 0.20. The BIC choice, single parenthood alone, is its most frequent choice, at 0.31. Figure 29.4.1 shows how often each regressor is included. Even single parenthood, whose t statistic in the chosen model is about 5.5, is left out by AIC in a fifth of the resamples. It is correlated −0.70 with the percentage of white residents, and the two can stand in for each other.

exm-sel-nested.title: Screening, then cross-validating
exm-sel-nested.html:
Take n=50 cases, 200 candidate regressors and a response that is independent of all of them, with σ=1. The procedure keeps the 5 regressors most correlated with the response and fits least squares on them. Every procedure has expected prediction error at least σ2=1 here. Over 200 data sets:

  • ten-fold cross-validation of the least squares fit, after screening on all the data, averages 0.720, and is below 1 in a fraction 0.93 of the data sets;
  • ten-fold cross-validation that repeats the screening inside every fold averages 1.427;
  • the actual prediction error of the screened and fitted model averages 1.372.

The wrong version reports that noise predicts the response. The right one is slightly pessimistic, because it uses 45 cases instead of 50 (@prp-sel-cv-target).

exm-sel-pretest-coverage.title: Coverage after a pretest
exm-sel-pretest-coverage.html:
Take two standardized regressors with correlation r, known σ, and the question: what is β1? The analyst first tests β2=0 at level 5%. If the test rejects, she reports the usual 95% interval for β1 from the model with both regressors; otherwise, the interval from the model with x1 alone. Each interval is correct for its own model. Panel (b) of Figure 29.5.1 shows the coverage of the reported interval as a function of δ=β2/sd(β^2), the standardized size of the coefficient being tested. When δ=0 the short model is correct and coverage is close to nominal. When δ is large the test always keeps x2 and coverage is nominal. In between, the test often drops x2 although the short slope is biased by rβ2 (@thm-dep-omitted), and the coverage falls to a minimum of 0.873 (at δ=2.2) for r=0.5, 0.599 (at δ=1.8) for r=0.8 and 0.234 (at δ=1.2) for r=0.95.

Panel (a) is the one-dimensional case of @prp-sel-selection-bias(c) with c=1.96: the conditional coverage is 0 at θ=0, 0.844 at θ=1, 0.951 at θ=2 and 0.971 at θ=3, where it slightly over-covers.

exm-sel-state-cp.title: Violent crime in the states
exm-sel-state-cp.html:
Return to the 50 states of Chapter 6 (the District of Columbia left out) and take as response the logarithm of the violent crime rate in 2009. The candidate regressors are the percentages of adults with a high-school diploma, of people below the poverty line, of single-parent households, of white residents and of urban residents, so there are 25=32 candidates, all with an intercept. The full model has P=6 and s2=0.1035. The eight candidates with the smallest Cp are

regressors p Cp ΔAIC ΔBIC R¯2
single, urban 3 2.20 0.00 0.42 0.471
poverty, single, urban 4 2.47 0.09 2.42 0.480
single 2 3.54 1.49 0.00 0.445
high school, single, urban 4 3.94 1.72 4.05 0.463
high school, poverty, single, urban 5 4.01 1.57 5.82 0.474
single, white, urban 4 4.04 1.82 4.16 0.462
poverty, single, white, urban 5 4.47 2.09 6.34 0.468
high school, single 3 5.48 3.42 3.85 0.434

where Δ is the difference from the smallest value over all 32 candidates. Cp and AIC choose single parenthood and urbanization; BIC drops urbanization; R¯2 adds poverty. The first three rows are within two units of each other on every scale, and none of the criteria separates them convincingly. Figure 29.2.1 is Mallows’ plot. Every candidate without single parenthood lies far above the line Cp=p: it is badly biased.

exm-sel-state-cv.title: Cross-validating the state regressions
exm-sel-state-cv.html: For each size from 0 to 5, take the best subset of the state regressors by residual sum of squares and estimate its prediction error by ten-fold cross-validation, with one random split into folds of five states. Figure 29.3.2 shows the result. The minimum, 0.1136 with standard error 0.0198, is at two regressors (single parenthood and urbanization), the choice of Cp and AIC. Single parenthood alone has 0.1162, well within one standard error, so the one-standard-error rule chooses it, the choice of BIC. The full model has 0.1351 and the intercept alone 0.1993. Leave-one-out over all 32 candidates gives 0.1129 for single parenthood and urbanization and 0.1130 for single parenthood alone, a tie, and 0.1184 for poverty with single parenthood and urbanization.

exm-sel-state-posi.title: Honest intervals for the state regressions
exm-sel-state-posi.title_html: Honest intervals for the state regressions
exm-sel-state-posi.html: For the state data, with the intercept always in, the 32 candidate models contain N=80 slope coefficients. Every vM,j is orthogonal to 1, so they span at most q=5 dimensions, and ν=44. The multipliers are 2.015 for the naive t interval, 3.12 for PoSI (by simulation), 3.484 for Scheffé and 3.684 for Bonferroni. In the model chosen by AIC, single parenthood and urbanization, the t statistics computed with the full-model s are 5.46 and 1.83. Single parenthood clears every multiplier. Urbanization clears none, not even the naive one: AIC kept it because its squared t exceeds about 2 (the threshold of Section 29.2), which is a decision about prediction, not evidence of an effect.

exm-sel-subset-df.title: Best subset of a given size
exm-sel-subset-df.title_html: Best subset of a given size
exm-sel-subset-df.html: Keep the k largest of m=20 values |Zj| and set the rest to zero, with Zj∼N(θj,1) independent. For a subset fixed in advance the degrees of freedom would be k. Figure 29.1.1 shows them by simulation. When all θj=0, the best single coordinate already costs 4.91 degrees of freedom, the best five cost 13.94 and the best ten 18.27. When five means equal 6 and the rest are zero, choosing the best five is almost free (5.06), because the five are obvious; choosing a sixth means choosing among fifteen pure-noise coordinates, and the degrees of freedom jump to 9.47. Searching among many candidates of equal merit is expensive, and choosing between clear winners and clear losers is cheap.

exm-sel-three-ways.title: Three ways to report after forward selection
exm-sel-three-ways.title_html: Three ways to report after forward selection
exm-sel-three-ways.html:
Take n=100 cases of ten normal regressors with pairwise correlations 0.5, σ=1, choose a model by forward selection with AIC, and report 95% intervals for the chosen coefficients, with the projection coefficients βM^,j as targets. Over 3000 data sets, the fraction of reported intervals that cover their targets is:

naive split in half Scheffé
no signal: coverage 0.440 0.946 1.000
no signal: mean half-width 0.228 0.351 0.516
three slopes of 0.3: coverage 0.868 0.956 1.000
three slopes of 0.3: mean half-width 0.248 0.379 0.559

With no signal, fewer than half of the naive intervals cover: a coefficient is reported only because its estimate was large. Splitting restores the nominal level at the cost of intervals about one and a half times as wide. The Scheffé intervals, with multiplier 10F0.05(10,89)=4.403, are valid for every model and every rule, and here they are very conservative, because forward selection explores only a small part of the 5120 coefficients they protect.

exm-sel-truncated.title: A selective interval
exm-sel-truncated.html: Let Z∼N(θ,1) be reported only when |Z|>1.96, and suppose Z=2.5 is observed. Given selection, Z has the normal distribution truncated to |z|>1.96. Let Fθ be its distribution function. Then Fθ(Z) is uniform on (0,1) given selection, whatever θ, and Fθ(z) decreases in θ (@exr-sel-trunc-monotone). So {θ:0.025≤Fθ(2.5)≤0.975} is an interval with conditional coverage exactly 95% for every θ. Numerically it is [−0.42,4.33], against the naive [0.54,4.46]. An estimate just past the threshold is weak evidence once the threshold is taken into account, and the selective interval includes zero.

exm-sel-wrong-mean.title: Optimism of a wrong model
exm-sel-wrong-mean.html: Take n=30 equally spaced points ti on [−1,1], a curved mean μi=1+ti+1.5ti2, σ=1, and fit by least squares a straight line in t together with two columns of pure noise, so p=4. The model is wrong: its squared bias per observation is 𝛍‖(I−M)μ‖2/n=0.2054. Over 20000 simulated data sets the average optimism is 0.2688, against 2σ2p/n=0.2667 from @thm-sel-optimism(c). Ridge regression (@thm-shr-ridge) on the same columns with penalty λ=5 is a linear smoother with tr(S)=3.207; its simulated optimism is 0.2163, against 2×3.207/30=0.2138 from part (b).

exr-sel-aic-cp.title: B1
exr-sel-aic-cp.html: Let σ^2 be any fixed positive number and write SSEk/n=σ^2(1+δk). Show that AICk−AICj=SSEk−SSEjσ^2+2(pk−pj)+nO(δk2+δj2), and conclude that with σ^2=s2 AIC and Cp differences agree when every candidate’s residual mean square is close to s2.

exr-sel-aic-limit.title: C1
exr-sel-aic-limit.html: In panel (a) of @exm-sel-aic-bic, suppose the three regressors with zero slopes are orthogonal to each other and to the relevant ones. Show that for large n AIC selects the true subset iff each of them has squared t statistic below about 2, and deduce the limit Pr{χ2(1)≤2}3.

exr-sel-aic-threshold.title: B3
exr-sel-aic-threshold.html: Show that AIC prefers the larger of two nested candidates iff F>(ν/q)(e2q/n−1), and BIC iff F>(ν/q)(nq/n−1). Find the limits of both thresholds as n→∞ with q and n−ν fixed.

exr-sel-backward-t.title: B3
exr-sel-backward-t.html: Show that a column’s F-to-remove in backward elimination is the square of its t statistic, and that backward elimination with Fout=tα/22(ν) is the rule “drop the least significant coefficient while any is not significant at level α”. Why do the p-values of the surviving coefficients not have their nominal meaning?

exr-sel-cond-cov.title: A1
exr-sel-cond-cov.html: In @prp-sel-selection-bias(c), take c=1.5<z0.025. Compute the conditional coverage at θ=0.

exr-sel-count.title: A1
exr-sel-count.html: How many subsets must exhaustive search examine for m=20 and m=40 candidate regressors? At a million subsets per second, how long does each take?

exr-sel-cp-hand.title: A1
exr-sel-cp-hand.html: In @exm-sel-state-cp the model with single parenthood and urbanization has SSE=4.782. Compute its Cp from s2, n and p, and the F statistic for testing it against the full model.

exr-sel-hard-risk.title: B2
exr-sel-hard-risk.html: Derive @eq-sel-hard-risk. (Split the risk according to whether the coordinate is kept, and use ∫abw2ϕ(w)dw=Φ(b)−Φ(a)−bϕ(b)+aϕ(a).)

exr-sel-holdout.title: A1
exr-sel-holdout.html: In @exm-sel-cv-bias, compute Err(20) from @thm-cor-prediction-error and confirm the value quoted for K=2. Why is a holdout estimate that fits on half the data especially biased when the number of regressors is large?

exr-sel-interpolate.title: A1
exr-sel-interpolate.html: The procedure 𝛍μ^(Y)=Y interpolates the data. Compute its training error, its in-sample prediction error and its degrees of freedom, and check @thm-sel-optimism(a).

exr-sel-loo-mean.title: B1
exr-sel-loo-mean.html: For the intercept-only model, show that the leave-one-out residual is n(yi−y¯)/(n−1) and that CVn=ns2/(n−1), where s2 is the sample variance. Check this against @thm-sel-loocv.

exr-sel-max-df.title: C2
exr-sel-max-df.html: In @exm-sel-subset-df with all θj=0 and k=1, show that the degrees of freedom equal EmaxjZj2 (with σ=1). Deduce that they are at least 1, and use EmaxjZj2≥(Emaxj|Zj|)2 to explain why they grow without bound as m→∞.

exr-sel-mills.title: B1
exr-sel-mills.html: In the orthonormal design of @prp-sel-orthonormal with σ=1 and a zero coefficient, show that E(|Zj|∣|Zj|>c)=ϕ(c)/(1−Φ(c)). Evaluate it for c=2 and c=1.96, and interpret it as the average size of a selected null coefficient.

exr-sel-moving-average.title: B2
exr-sel-moving-average.html: Arrange n observations on a circle, and let μ^i be the average of Yi−q,…,Yi+q (indices modulo n, 2q+1≤n). Find the degrees of freedom and the expected optimism, and explain why a wider window is “simpler”.

exr-sel-no-cycle.title: B2
exr-sel-no-cycle.html: In stepwise regression, show that the column just entered has F-to-remove equal to its F-to-enter. Deduce that it cannot be removed at the next step if Fout≤Fin, and explain what can happen if Fout>Fin.

exr-sel-not-nested.title: C1
exr-sel-not-nested.html: In @exm-sel-forward-miss, show that the best subset of size one is {x3} and the best of size two is {x1,x2}, so the best subsets of consecutive sizes need not be nested. Why does this not contradict @thm-proj-nested?

exr-sel-posi-count.title: B2
exr-sel-posi-count.html: Verify that the 32 candidate models of @exm-sel-state-posi contain 80 slope coefficients, and that every vM,j for a slope is orthogonal to 1. Why does this let Scheffé’s bound use q=5 instead of 6?

exr-sel-pretest-formula.title: C2
exr-sel-pretest-formula.html: In @exm-sel-pretest-coverage, let β^1S be the short slope and β^2 the long-model estimate of β2. Use @lem-dep-short-long to show that the two are independent, and write the coverage of the reported interval as Pr(|T2|≤z)Pr(|β^1S−β1|≤zsd(β^1S))+Pr(|T2|>z, |β^1−β1|≤zsd(β^1)), where T2=β^2/sd(β^2). Explain why only the first term depends on the bias rβ2 of the short slope in this simple way.

exr-sel-ridge-df.title: B1
exr-sel-ridge-df.html: Let Sλ=X(X⊤X+λI)−1X⊤ be the ridge smoother, whose trace ∑jdj2/(dj2+λ) was found in @thm-shr-ridge. Show that tr(SλSλ⊤)<tr(Sλ) for every λ>0 with X≠0, and that for a symmetric smoother S with eigenvalues in [0,1], tr(SS⊤)=tr(S) iff S is an orthogonal projection.

exr-sel-ridge-leverage.title: B2
exr-sel-ridge-leverage.html: In @thm-sel-loocv, suppose X has full column rank. Show that sii≤hii, where hii is the least squares leverage, so that the shortcut inflates ridge residuals less than least squares residuals.

exr-sel-stone.title: C2
exr-sel-stone.html: Suppose maxi|hii−p/n|≤ϵp/n. Show that SSEn(1−pn(1+ϵ))−2 ≥ CVn ≥ SSEn(1−pn(1−ϵ))−2, and deduce that nlog⁡CVn=nlog⁡(SSE/n)+2p+O(pϵ+p2/n). Which designs satisfy the hypothesis with small ϵ?

exr-sel-sure-choose.title: C1
exr-sel-sure-choose.html: In the sequence model Zj∼N(θj,σ2), j=1,…,p, independent, soft thresholding at λ has Stein’s unbiased risk estimate SURE(λ)=∑j=1pmin(Zj2,λ2)−pσ2+2σ2#{j:|Zj|>λ} by @prp-sel-divergence, because Zj−θ^j is Zj when |Zj|≤λ and ±λ otherwise. Let 0=a0≤a1≤⋯≤ap be 0 and the ordered |Zj|. Show that SURE is nondecreasing on each interval [ak,ak+1), so it is minimized over λ≥0 at one of a0,…,ap. Compute SURE(0), and explain why the minimized value is biased downwards. (Minimizing SURE is the SureShrink rule of Donoho and Johnstone 1995.)

exr-sel-tree.title: B1
exr-sel-tree.html: Show that in the tree of @prp-sel-branch-bound every subset of {1,…,m} is reached along exactly one path from the root, and that the descendants of (S,ℓ) are exactly the subsets T with F⊆T⊆S.

exr-sel-trunc-monotone.title: C1
exr-sel-trunc-monotone.html: Let Fθ be the distribution function of N(θ,1) truncated to a set A of positive probability. Show that for θ1<θ2 the density ratio fθ2(z)/fθ1(z) is increasing in z∈A, and deduce that Fθ2(z)≤Fθ1(z) for every z. Why does this make the set in @exm-sel-truncated an interval?

exr-sel-unequal-folds.title: C1
exr-sel-unequal-folds.html: Generalize @prp-sel-cv-target to folds of unequal sizes n1,…,nK, and to leave-one-out for a design that is fixed rather than random. In the fixed-design case, what does E(CVn) equal for least squares, and how does it compare with the in-sample prediction error of @thm-sel-optimism?

prp-sel-adjusted-link.title: Adjusted R^2 as a criterion
prp-sel-adjusted-link.title_html: Adjusted R2 as a criterion
prp-sel-adjusted-link.html: Maximizing R¯2 over candidates that contain the intercept is minimizing sk2=SSEk/(n−pk), and for two nested candidates the larger has the larger R¯2 iff its added columns have F>1.

prp-sel-aic-bic.title: AIC and BIC in large samples
prp-sel-aic-bic.title_html: AIC and BIC in large samples
prp-sel-aic-bic.html:
Let the candidate set K be finite and fixed, and consider a sequence of designs and means with n→∞. Let the errors be independent and identically distributed with mean zero and variance σ2, and let 𝛍supn‖μ‖2/n<∞. Call k correct if 𝛍μ∈C(Xk). Assume that there is a correct k0 such that every other correct candidate has pk>pk0, and that 𝛍lim infn‖(I−Mk)μ‖2/n>0 for every candidate that is not correct. Select k^ by minimizing ICk=nlog⁡(SSEk/n)+cnpk.

  1. If cn→∞ and cn/n→0, then Pr(k^=k0)→1. In particular BIC (cn=log⁡n) is consistent.

  2. If cn=c is constant, the errors are normal, and k is a correct candidate with C(Xk0)⊂C(Xk) and q=pk−pk0, then Pr(ICk<ICk0)→Pr{χ2(q)>cq}>0. In particular AIC (c=2) is not consistent when such a candidate is available.

  3. (Efficiency, stated with a sketch.) Suppose instead that no candidate is correct, and that the candidate sets grow with n so that the smallest risk over candidates tends to infinity. Then, under moment conditions on the errors and a condition limiting the number of candidates, with σ2 known or consistently estimated in Cp, and for AIC with the largest candidate dimension o(n), the loss 𝛍𝛍‖μ^k^−μ‖2 of the Cp or AIC choice divided by 𝛍𝛍mink‖μ^k−μ‖2 tends to one in probability (Shibata 1981; Li 1987). A criterion with cn→∞ does not have this property in general.

prp-sel-branch-bound.title: Branch and bound for C_p
prp-sel-branch-bound.title_html: Branch and bound for Cp
prp-sel-branch-bound.html: Let c∗ be the smallest Cp found so far. If a node (S,ℓ) satisfies SSESs2−n+2(|F|+1) ≥ c∗, then no descendant of the node has Cp<c∗, and the node need not be expanded. A depth-first search that evaluates every expanded node and skips such nodes’ descendants returns a subset of minimal Cp.

prp-sel-cp.title: Properties of C_p
prp-sel-cp.title_html: Properties of Cp
prp-sel-cp.html:
1. Under @eq-sel-model, Ckσ=SSEk/σ2−n+2pk is unbiased for Jk.

  2. Assume normal errors, 𝛍μ∈C(XF), C(Xk)⊆C(XF) and n−P>2. Then E(Ck)=Jk+2(P−pk+γk)n−P−2.

  3. Let Fk=[(SSEk−SSEF)/(P−pk)]/s2 be the F statistic for testing candidate k against the full model (pk<P). Then Ck=(P−pk)(Fk−1)+pk. In particular CF=P, and Ck≤pk iff Fk≤1.

prp-sel-cv-target.title: What K-fold cross-validation estimates
prp-sel-cv-target.html: Let the cases be independent draws of (X,Y), let the folds be fixed in advance with equal sizes n/K, and let Err(m)=E(Y0−f^m(X0))2 be the expected squared error of the procedure fitted to m cases, for an independent new case (X0,Y0). Then E(CVK)=Err(n−n/K).

prp-sel-divergence.title: Degrees of freedom as a divergence
prp-sel-divergence.title_html: Degrees of freedom as a divergence
prp-sel-divergence.html: Let 𝛍Y∼Nn(μ,σ2I). Suppose that for each i, for almost every value of the other coordinates, yi↦μ^i(y) is absolutely continuous, and that E|∂μ^i/∂yi| and Eμ^i2 are finite. Then 𝛍df(μ^)=E∑i=1n∂μ^i∂yi(Y), and err―+2σ2n−1∑i∂μ^i/∂yi is an unbiased estimate of E(Errin) that does not involve 𝛍μ.

prp-sel-forward-step.title: What a stepwise step maximizes
prp-sel-forward-step.html:
Let y~=(I−MS)y and x~j=(I−MS)xj≠0, and let rj=y~⊤x~j/(‖y~‖‖x~j‖) be the partial correlation of y and xj given the columns of S (@def-cor-sample-partial).

  1. SSES−SSES+j=rj2SSES and Fj=(n−pS−1)rj2/(1−rj2). So the column that most reduces SSE is the one with the largest rj2, the largest F-to-enter, and the smallest Cp, AIC or BIC of the enlarged model.

  2. For j∈S, SSES−j−SSES=tj2sS2, where tj is the t statistic of xj in the model S and sS2=SSES/(n−pS). So backward elimination removes the column with the smallest |tj|, and its F-to-remove is tj2.

prp-sel-hard-df.title: Degrees of freedom of hard thresholding
prp-sel-hard-df.title_html: Degrees of freedom of hard thresholding
prp-sel-hard-df.html: Let Z∼N(θ,σ2) and λ>0. Then Cov(Z1{|Z|>λ},Z)σ2=Pr(|Z|>λ)+λσ[ϕ(λ−θσ)+ϕ(λ+θσ)], where ϕ is the standard normal density.

prp-sel-orthonormal.title: Selection as hard thresholding
prp-sel-orthonormal.html: Let X have orthonormal columns, X⊤X=Im, put Z=X⊤Y, and let σ2 be known. Among all subsets S of the columns, SSES/σ2+c2|S| is minimized (uniquely, with probability one) by S={j:|Zj|>cσ}. The selected fit has coefficients Zj1{|Zj|>cσ}.

prp-sel-same-size.title: One size, one ranking
prp-sel-same-size.html: Among candidates with the same number of columns p, the orderings by Cp, AIC, AICc, BIC, R2, R¯2 and SSE coincide.

prp-sel-selection-bias.title: What selection does to estimates and intervals
prp-sel-selection-bias.title_html: What selection does to estimates and intervals
prp-sel-selection-bias.html:
1. (Selected maxima are biased upwards.) Let Z1,…,Zm have finite means θ1,…,θm, and let J^ be an index at which ZJ^=maxjZj. Then E(ZJ^) ≥ maxjθj ≥ E(θJ^), so E(ZJ^−θJ^)≥0. If the Zj are independent N(θ,1) with a common mean and m≥2, the bias is EmaxjZj−θ>0.

  2. (Selected minima of risk estimates are optimistic.) Let R^k be an unbiased estimate of Rk for each candidate k in a finite set, and let k^ minimize R^k. Then E(R^k^) ≤ minkRk ≤ E(Rk^).

  3. (Selected intervals under-cover.) Let Z∼N(θ,1), and report the interval Z±zα/2 only when |Z|>c. If c≥zα/2, the probability that the reported interval covers θ, given that it is reported, is 0 at θ=0. It tends to 1−α as |θ|→∞.

prp-sel-simultaneous.title: Simultaneous inference over submodels
prp-sel-simultaneous.html:
Assume the normal model @eq-opt-normal-model with rank(X)=P<n, let s2 be the full-model estimate with ν=n−P, and let M be a collection of column subsets M with XM of full column rank. For M∈M and j∈M let vM,j=XM(XM⊤XM)−1ej, where ej picks out the coefficient of xj, and 𝛃βM,j=vM,j⊤Xβ,β^M,j=vM,j⊤Y, and for K>0 let IM,j(K)=[β^M,j±Ks‖vM,j‖]. Let N be the number of pairs (M,j) and q the dimension of the span of the vM,j.

  1. With K=qFα(q,ν), Pr(βM,j∈IM,j(K) for all M∈M, j∈M)≥1−α.

  2. The same holds with K=tα/(2N)(ν).

  3. If K has the property in (a), then for every selection rule M^ with values in M, a function of Y that may also depend on the unknown 𝛃β and σ, Pr(βM^,j∈IM^,j(K) for all j∈M^)≥1−α.

  4. The smallest K with the property in (c) for every such rule, including rules that depend on the unknown parameters (the convention of Berk, Brown, Buja, Zhang and Zhao 2013), is KPoSI, the 1−α quantile of 𝛃maxM,j|vM,j⊤(Y−Xβ)|/(s‖vM,j‖), whose distribution does not depend on 𝛃β or σ.

prp-sel-splitting.title: Sample splitting
prp-sel-splitting.html: Let Y=(Y1⊤,Y2⊤)⊤, where 𝛍Y2∼Nn2(μ2,σ2I) is independent of Y1, and let X2 be the fixed design of the second part. Let M^ be any rule that chooses a set of columns from Y1 (and the design), with values in the set of M for which X2,M has full column rank pM<n2. For each such M, let 𝛃𝛍βM=(X2,M⊤X2,M)−1X2,M⊤μ2, and let IM,j be the usual level 1−α t interval for the jth coefficient from the least squares fit of Y2 on X2,M. Then, given Y1, IM^,j covers βM^,j with probability at least 1−α, with equality if 𝛍μ2∈C(X2,M^). The same holds unconditionally.

thm-sel-aicc.title: The expected discrepancy of a normal linear model
thm-sel-aicc.title_html: The expected discrepancy of a normal linear model
thm-sel-aicc.html:
Let 𝛍Y∼Nn(μ,σ2I) with 𝛍μ∈C(Xk) and n>pk+2, and let σ^k2=SSEk/n. For the fitted density 𝛍Nn(μ^k,σ^k2I), E(Δk)=E[nlog⁡(2πσ^k2)]+n(n+pk)n−pk−2. Consequently AICck=−2ℓk+2(pk+1)+2(pk+1)(pk+2)n−pk−2{#eq-sel-aicc}

is an unbiased estimate of E(Δk).

thm-sel-loocv.title: Leave-one-out without refitting
thm-sel-loocv.html:
Let Ω be a p×p nonnegative definite matrix, let 𝛃β^ minimize ‖y−Xb‖2+b⊤Ωb, and let 𝛃β^(i) minimize the same criterion with case i removed. Assume that A(i)=X(i)⊤X(i)+Ω is nonsingular for every i, where X(i) is X without row i. Let S=X(X⊤X+Ω)−1X⊤ and y^=Sy. Then:

  1. sii<1 for every i;

  2. 𝛃yi−x(i)⊤β^(i)=(yi−y^i)/(1−sii);

  3. consequently CVn=1n∑i=1n(yi−y^i1−sii)2.{#eq-sel-loo-shortcut}

For least squares (Ω=0) this is @thm-res-deletion(d), and CVn=PRESS/n with PRESS as in @eq-res-press.

thm-sel-optimism.title: Optimism is a covariance
thm-sel-optimism.html:
Under @eq-sel-model, let 𝛍μ^ be a fitting procedure.

  1. The expected optimism is ω=2n∑i=1nCov(μ^i,Yi).

  2. If 𝛍μ^=SY for a fixed n×n matrix S, then ω=2σ2tr(S)/n and 𝛍𝛍𝛍E‖μ^−μ‖2=‖(I−S)μ‖2+σ2tr(SS⊤).

  3. For least squares on a model matrix X of rank p, whether or not 𝛍μ∈C(X), 𝛍𝛍E(err―)=σ2n−pn+‖(I−M)μ‖2n,E(Errin)=σ2n+pn+‖(I−M)μ‖2n, and ω=2σ2p/n.
